data.title: Key Organic Reactions I: Substitution
data.summary: This lesson explains the three main types of substitution reactions in organic chemistry: SN1, SN2, and electrophilic aromatic substitution. Students will learn the step‑by‑step mechanisms, the conditions that favor each pathway, and how to predict the products.
objectives: Describe the stepwise mechanism of SN1 and identify the carbocation intermediate
Explain the concerted mechanism of SN2 and illustrate the backside attack
Outline the electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) mechanism and the role of the aromatic ring
Predict which reaction conditions (solvent, nucleophile/base strength, temperature) favor SN1, SN2, or EAS
Draw complete reaction mechanisms for given substrates
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic covalent bonding, functional groups, and the concept of nucleophiles and electrophiles.
why: Organic substitution reactions are the foundation of how many pharmaceuticals, polymers, and agrochemicals are made. Knowing which pathway a reaction follows lets chemists design efficient syntheses and avoid unwanted side products.

In everyday life, the flavors in food, the fragrances in perfumes, and the durability of plastics all depend on controlled substitution reactions. Understanding these mechanisms helps future scientists improve existing products and create new, safer materials.

sections.heading: Review of Nucleophiles, Electrophiles, and Leaving Groups
sections.body:
Nucleophiles and electrophiles are the two partners that meet in a substitution reaction.  
Think of a dance: one dancer reaches out to give a hand (the nucleophile) while the other opens a space on the floor (the electrophile). The hand‑giver must have something to “give,” and the floor‑opener must have a spot that can be left behind.

**Nucleophile** – a species that **donates** a pair of electrons to form a new bond.  
The word comes from *nucleus* (center) and *phile* (loving), so a nucleophile “loves” positively charged or electron‑poor places. In chemistry this means it has a lone pair of electrons or a negative charge that it can share.

**Electrophile** – a species that **accepts** a pair of electrons.  
*Electro* means “electric,” and *phile* again means “loving,” so an electrophile “loves” electrons. It is usually a carbon atom that carries a partial positive charge because the atoms attached to it pull electron density away.

When a nucleophile meets an electrophile, the nucleophile’s electron pair moves toward the electrophile, creating a new bond. In a substitution reaction, something else must leave the electrophilic carbon at the same time; otherwise the carbon would end up with five bonds, which is impossible.

> **Definition:** A **leaving group** is the part of a molecule that departs with the electron pair it originally shared with the carbon atom. It becomes a separate, stable species after the bond breaks.

Why does the leaving group matter? Imagine you are trying to open a door. If the hinge is rusted, the door will not swing open easily. A good leaving group is like a well‑lubricated hinge: it can break away smoothly, allowing the nucleophile to slide in. A poor leaving group is like a stuck hinge; the reaction slows down or stops because the bond is too hard to break.

Common leaving groups in organic chemistry include:

| Leaving group | Why it leaves well |
|--------------|--------------------|
| Halides (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) | Large, polarizable ions that can stabilize the negative charge after departure |
| Tosylate (OTs) | Resonance‑stabilized sulfonate anion; spreads the charge over several atoms |
| Water (H₂O) | Forms when an –OH group is first protonated; neutral water is a very stable molecule |
| Alkoxide (RO⁻) – *poor* | Strong base, holds onto its electrons tightly, so it does not leave easily unless converted to a better group (e.g., by protonation) |

The ability of a leaving group is measured by how stable the species is after it leaves. The more stable, the better it can “accept” the electron pair that used to belong to the carbon. This stability often comes from:

* **Charge delocalization** – the negative charge can be spread over several atoms (as in tosylate).  
* **Size and polarizability** – larger ions like I⁻ can hold the charge more comfortably.  
* **Resonance** – multiple ways to draw the electrons make the leaving group less reactive.

> **Note:** A good leaving group is usually a weak base. Strong bases hold onto electrons tightly and therefore do not leave easily.

In substitution mechanisms (SN1 and SN2) the rate at which the leaving group departs controls the overall speed of the reaction. If the leaving group is poor, the nucleophile may never get a chance to attack, and the reaction will be very slow or require harsh conditions (high temperature, strong acid, etc.). Conversely, with an excellent leaving group, the reaction can proceed quickly at room temperature.

> **In daily life:** Think of a taxi (nucleophile) picking up a passenger (electrophilic carbon). The passenger can only get into the taxi if the previous rider (leaving group) gets out smoothly. If the door is jammed, the new passenger must wait longer.

> **Remember:** When you see a substitution reaction, always ask three questions:  
> 1. Who is the nucleophile (electron donor)?  
> 2. Who is the electrophile (electron acceptor)?  
> 3. How good is the leaving group that must depart?

Understanding these three roles lets you predict whether a reaction will happen easily and which mechanism (stepwise SN1 or concerted SN2) is more likely.

sections.heading: SN1 Mechanism: Stepwise Substitution
sections.body:
When a molecule undergoes an **SN1 reaction**, the substitution does not happen all at once.  
Instead, the bond between the carbon atom and the leaving group breaks first, creating a positively‑charged carbon called a **carbocation**.  
Only after this intermediate exists does the nucleophile— the species that wants to give its pair of electrons— rush in and attach to the carbocation.  

> **Definition:** *SN1* stands for **Substitution Nucleophilic Unimolecular**. “Unimolecular” means the slow, rate‑determining step involves only one molecule (the substrate that is losing its leaving group).

### Step 1 – Formation of the carbocation  

1. The carbon‑leaving‑group bond is polarized because the leaving group is more electronegative; it pulls electron density toward itself.  
2. In a polar solvent (especially one that can stabilize charges, such as water or alcohols), the bond can break more easily. The solvent molecules surround the leaving group and the emerging carbocation, lowering the energy needed for the break‑away.  
3. When the bond finally snaps, the leaving group departs with the pair of electrons it owned, becoming a **leaving group anion**. The carbon is left with only three bonds and carries a positive charge: a **carbocation**.

$$\text{R–LG} \;\xrightarrow{\text{polar solvent}}\; \text{R}^{+} + \text{LG}^{-}$$  

The speed of this first step decides how fast the whole reaction goes. Because only one molecule is involved, the rate law is first‑order:  

$$\text{rate} = k[\text{R–LG}]$$  

### Step 2 – Nucleophilic attack  

1. The nucleophile (denoted Nu⁻) approaches the planar carbocation.  
2. Because the carbocation is electron‑deficient, the nucleophile donates its lone pair to form a new bond.  
3. The result is the substituted product, and the solvent may later remove a proton if the nucleophile was neutral (e.g., water giving an alcohol).

$$\text{R}^{+} + \text{Nu}^{-} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R–Nu}$$  

### Why carbocation stability matters  

Carbocations are not equally stable. Their stability follows a clear trend:

- **Tertiary (3°) > Secondary (2°) > Primary (1°) > Methyl**  

The reason is **hyperconjugation** and **inductive effects**: more alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon can donate electron density through σ‑bonds, spreading out the positive charge and lowering the energy.  

> **Note:** A tertiary carbocation can also rearrange (shift a hydrogen or alkyl group) to become even more stable before the nucleophile attacks. This explains why some SN1 products look different from the starting material.

### Role of solvent polarity  

A polar, protic solvent (one that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds) stabilizes ions through solvation. Think of the solvent as a crowd of friendly people that surround and “hold hands” with the charged species, making it easier for the leaving group to leave and for the carbocation to exist. In a non‑polar solvent, the energy barrier to form the carbocation is much higher, and SN1 reactions are sluggish or do not occur.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a crowded party where a guest (the leaving group) wants to leave the room. If the room is full of helpful friends (polar solvent), the guest can quickly find a hand to guide them out, leaving an empty chair (carbocation). Once the chair is empty, another guest (the nucleophile) can sit down without bumping anyone else.

### Putting it together  

1. **Leave first:** The substrate loses its leaving group, forming a carbocation.  
2. **Solve the charge:** The polar solvent stabilizes the charged pieces, making the break easier.  
3. **Invite the nucleophile:** The nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation, giving the final product.  

> **Remember:** In SN1, the rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, not on the nucleophile, because the slow step is the formation of the carbocation.  

Understanding these steps helps you predict when a reaction will follow the SN1 pathway—typically with a good leaving group, a stable (often tertiary) carbocation, and a polar protic solvent.

sections.heading: SN2 Mechanism: Concerted Substitution
sections.body:
When we talk about an **SN2 reaction**, we mean a single, smooth “hand‑off” of a leaving group by a nucleophile.  
The word **SN2** stands for *substitution nucleophilic bimolecular*: two species (the nucleophile and the substrate) are involved in the rate‑determining step, and the reaction proceeds by substitution.

> **Definition:** *SN2* is a one‑step, concerted substitution where the nucleophile attacks from the opposite side of the leaving group, forming a transition state that contains both bonds at once.

---

### The idea in plain words  

Imagine you are swapping a seat on a crowded bus. A passenger (the nucleophile) wants to sit where another passenger (the leaving group) is standing. The new passenger steps in from the opposite side of the aisle, pushes the standing passenger out, and both are never in the bus at the same time. In chemistry, the nucleophile “steps in” while the leaving group “steps out” in a single motion.

---

### Why the backside attack?  

The nucleophile approaches the carbon atom that bears the leaving group **from the side opposite the leaving group**. This direction is called the *backside* because it is the side where the electron pair of the leaving group is pointing away. Approaching from the front would force the two electron pairs to clash, which is energetically unfavorable.  

In the transition state, the carbon is **pentavalent**—it is partially bonded to both the nucleophile and the leaving group at the same time. The geometry is roughly a flat, five‑membered arrangement called a *trigonal bipyramidal* transition state. The two bonds being formed and broken lie 180° apart, giving the classic “in‑line” picture:

$$
\text{Nu}^- \; \longrightarrow \; \underset{\text{transition state}}{\overset{\displaystyle \angle 180^\circ}{\text{C}}} \; \text{LG}
$$

Here “Nu” is the nucleophile, “LG” is the leaving group, and the arrow shows the direction of attack.

---

### How steric hindrance slows the reaction  

**Steric hindrance** means that bulky groups block the space around the reactive carbon. Because the nucleophile must come straight in from the backside, any large substituents near that side act like a crowded doorway, making it harder for the nucleophile to reach the carbon.  

If the carbon is attached to three small groups (a *primary* carbon), the doorway is wide open and the SN2 reaction is fast. If the carbon is attached to two or three large groups (secondary or tertiary), the doorway narrows, and the reaction slows dramatically or stops. This is why SN2 reactions are rarely observed at tertiary carbons.

> **Note:** The rate law for an SN2 reaction is *second order*:  
> $$\text{rate} = k[\text{Nu}^-][\text{R–LG}]$$  
> Both the nucleophile and the substrate concentration matter because both must collide in the correct orientation.

---

### Nucleophile strength matters  

A **nucleophile** is a species that donates an electron pair to form a new bond. Strong nucleophiles have high electron density and are usually negatively charged (e.g., $ \text{OH}^- $, $ \text{CN}^- $) or neutral but highly polarizable (e.g., $ \text{I}^- $, $ \text{SMe}^- $). Because the SN2 step requires the nucleophile to attack directly, a stronger nucleophile can push into the transition state more effectively, increasing the reaction rate.

In contrast, a weak nucleophile (like water or methanol) donates electrons less readily, so the reaction proceeds more slowly, even if steric hindrance is low.

> **In daily life:** Think of a strong nucleophile as a confident person pushing through a crowd to reach a seat, while a weak nucleophile is shy and hesitates, taking longer to get there.

---

### Putting it together  

1. **Backside attack** gives the correct orbital overlap for the carbon–nucleophile bond to form while the carbon–leaving‑group bond breaks.  
2. The **transition state** is a fleeting, five‑coordinate structure where the carbon is stretched between the two partners.  
3. **Steric hindrance** blocks the backside, slowing or preventing the reaction.  
4. **Nucleophile strength** determines how readily the nucleophile can make the attack; stronger nucleophiles give faster SN2 reactions.

> **Remember:** SN2 needs a clear backside and a good nucleophile. If either is missing, the reaction will be sluggish or will follow a different pathway (like SN1).

sections.heading: Comparing SN1 and SN2: When Does Each Occur?
sections.body:
When you look at a substitution reaction, the first question is **which path will the molecule take?**  
The two most common routes are **SN1** and **SN2**. Both replace a leaving group (a part of the molecule that can depart, like a chloride ion) with a nucleophile (an atom or group that donates a pair of electrons). The difference lies in how many steps are involved and what the molecule “feels” during the process.

> **Definition:** **SN1** = “Substitution Nucleophilic unimolecular”. One molecule (the substrate) decides the rate‑determining step.  
> **Definition:** **SN2** = “Substitution Nucleophilic bimolecular”. Two molecules (the substrate and the nucleophile) collide in the rate‑determining step.

Why does this matter? Knowing which mechanism is favored lets you predict the product’s shape (called **stereochemistry**) and how fast the reaction will go. In the lab, you can choose conditions that steer the reaction toward the outcome you want.

### Everyday comparison
Think of a **SN2** reaction like a **handshake**: two people must meet at the same time, grab each other’s hands, and then let go of the old partner. If one person is very busy (a weak nucleophile) or the room is crowded (a bulky substrate), the handshake is hard to make.  

A **SN1** reaction is more like **changing seats at a dinner table**. First, one person (the leaving group) gets up and leaves the seat, creating an empty chair (a carbocation). Then, after a short pause, another guest (the nucleophile) sits down. The first step—leaving the chair—controls how fast the whole process is.

### Factors that decide the path
The table below gathers the three most important factors: the **type of substrate**, the **solvent**, and the **strength of the nucleophile**.  

| Factor | Favors SN1 | Favors SN2 |
|--------|------------|------------|
| **Substrate (carbon attached to leaving group)** | Tertiary > Secondary > Primary; stable carbocation needed | Primary > Secondary; little steric hindrance |
| **Solvent** | Polar protic (e.g., water, alcohol) stabilizes ions | Polar aprotic (e.g., acetone, DMSO) does not solvate nucleophile strongly |
| **Nucleophile strength** | Weak nucleophile (e.g., water, alcohol) works because carbocation is already formed | Strong nucleophile (e.g., $I^-$, $CN^-$, $OH^-$) needed for the single concerted step |

> **Note:** A **polar protic** solvent can form hydrogen bonds, which helps to stabilize charged intermediates like carbocations. A **polar aprotic** solvent cannot hydrogen‑bond, so it leaves the nucleophile “naked” and more reactive.

### Example reactions

1. **Primary substrate (1‑bromopropane) – SN2**  
   $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{acetone}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaBr}$$  
   Here the nucleophile $I^-$ is strong, the solvent acetone is polar aprotic, and the carbon bearing the bromide is only attached to one other carbon, so there is little crowding. The reaction proceeds in one concerted step, inverting the configuration at carbon (if it were chiral).

2. **Secondary substrate (2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane) – mixed but often SN1**  
   $$\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{water}} \text{(CH}_3)_2\text{COHCH}_3 + \text{HBr}$$  
   The carbon is attached to two other carbons, giving a relatively stable carbocation. Water is a weak nucleophile in a polar protic medium, so the reaction follows the two‑step SN1 pathway.

3. **Tertiary substrate (tert‑butyl chloride) – SN1**  
   $$\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{CCl} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{methanol}} \text{(CH}_3)_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{Cl}^-$$  
   The tertiary carbon forms a very stable carbocation after the chloride leaves. Methanol is a weak nucleophile, and the polar protic environment stabilizes the intermediate, making SN1 the dominant route.

> **Remember:** If the substrate is **primary** and the nucleophile is **strong**, think SN2. If the substrate can **stabilize a carbocation** (secondary with resonance, tertiary) and the solvent is **polar protic**, think SN1.

### Quick checklist
- **Is the carbon crowded?** → Crowded → SN1; Open → SN2.  
- **What solvent are you using?** → Protic → SN1; Aprotic → SN2.  
- **How strong is the nucleophile?** → Weak → SN1; Strong → SN2.

By matching your reaction conditions to these clues, you can reliably predict whether a substitution will follow the SN1 or SN2 route, and thus control the product you obtain.

sections.heading: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) Overview
sections.body:
The aromatic ring (for example, benzene) is unusually stable because its six π‑electrons are spread out over the whole ring in a pattern called **aromaticity**.  
Even though the ring is stable, the cloud of π‑electrons can act as a **nucleophile** – a species that donates electrons. In an **electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS)** reaction, an electrophile (an electron‑poor species) attacks the π‑cloud, temporarily breaking the aromatic system, and then the ring regains its aromaticity after a proton is removed.

### Why the ring can be a nucleophile
Think of the π‑cloud as a flat, soft cushion that can be pressed down by a small, hard ball. The ball represents the electrophile; the cushion represents the electron density that the ball can push into. When the ball lands on the cushion, the cushion deforms (the aromatic ring is temporarily “broken”), but once the ball is removed and the cushion springs back, the original shape is restored. This “spring back” step is what makes the overall process a substitution rather than a destruction of the ring.

### The three stages of EAS

1. **π‑Complex formation (the attack)**  
   The electrophile approaches the aromatic ring and forms a weak, reversible bond with one carbon atom of the ring. This step is often called the *σ‑complex* or *Wheland intermediate* after the bond is fully formed.  
   $$\text{Ar–H} + \text{E}^+ \;\rightleftharpoons\; \text{Ar–E}^+$$  
   Here, *Ar–H* is the aromatic compound, *E⁺* is the electrophile, and *Ar–E⁺* is the positively charged intermediate.

2. **σ‑Complex (the carbocation)**  
   In this intermediate, the carbon that received the electrophile now carries a positive charge (a **carbocation**) because it has lost part of its aromatic stabilization. The ring is no longer aromatic at this point; the positive charge is delocalized over the adjacent carbons, which helps to spread out the instability.

3. **Deprotonation (restoring aromaticity)**  
   A base (often the solvent or a weakly basic anion present in the reaction mixture) removes a hydrogen atom from the carbon next to the one that received the electrophile. The electrons from the C–H bond flow back into the ring, re‑forming the continuous π‑system and restoring aromaticity. The final product is the original ring with a new substituent in place of the removed hydrogen.  
   $$\text{Ar–E}^+ \;-\; \text{H}^+ \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Ar–E} + \text{H}^+$$  

> **Definition:** *Electrophilic aromatic substitution* is a reaction where an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring, while the ring regains its aromatic character after the substitution.

### Common electrophiles used in EAS
- **Halogen cations** (e.g., $ \text{Br}_2 $ in the presence of a Lewis acid like FeBr₃) – give bromobenzene.  
- **Nitronium ion** $ \text{NO}_2^+ $ (generated from $ \text{HNO}_3 $ + $ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 $) – gives nitrobenzene.  
- **Sulfonyl cation** $ \text{SO}_3 $ (often as $ \text{SO}_3\cdot\text{Py} $) – gives benzenesulfonic acid.  
- **Acyl cation** $ \text{RCO}^+ $ (from an acid chloride + AlCl₃) – gives an acyl‑substituted aromatic (Friedel‑Crafts acylation).  

> **In daily life:** The production of many plastics, dyes, and pharmaceuticals starts with EAS reactions. For instance, the synthesis of nylon‑6,6 involves nitration of benzene to make nitrobenzene, which is later reduced to aniline.

> **Remember:** The aromatic ring must stay aromatic at the end of the reaction; any step that permanently destroys the π‑system (such as adding two substituents without deprotonation) does not belong to the EAS family.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that any electrophile will react with benzene. In reality, the electrophile must be strong enough to overcome the stability of the aromatic π‑system, and a Lewis acid catalyst is often required to generate a sufficiently reactive electrophile.  

By visualizing the aromatic ring as a flexible cushion that can temporarily accommodate a guest (the electrophile) and then bounce back to its original shape, the concept of electrophilic aromatic substitution becomes easier to grasp. The three‑step sequence—π‑complex formation, σ‑complex, and deprotonation—ensures that the ring ends up unchanged in its aromatic nature, but with a new substituent attached.

sections.heading: Factors Controlling EAS Reactivity and Orientation
sections.body:
In electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) a positively‑charged species, called an **electrophile**, attacks the aromatic ring and replaces a hydrogen atom.  
The speed of this reaction and the position where the new group ends up are not random – they are controlled by the other groups already attached to the ring.  

> **Definition:** *Activating group* – a substituent that makes the aromatic ring more reactive toward electrophiles, usually by donating electron density to the ring.  
> **Definition:** *Deactivating group* – a substituent that makes the ring less reactive toward electrophiles, usually by pulling electron density away from the ring.

### Why do some groups activate and others deactivate?

Think of the aromatic ring as a playground where the electrophile wants to join. If the playground is full of friendly kids (electron‑rich), the newcomer is welcomed quickly. If the playground is quiet and the kids are shy (electron‑poor), the newcomer has a hard time finding a spot.  

Electron‑donating groups (EDGs) such as –OH, –OCH₃, –NH₂, and alkyl groups push electrons toward the ring through **resonance** (delocalization of electrons across adjacent atoms) or **inductive** effects (through‑bond polarization). This raises the electron density of the ring, stabilising the positively‑charged intermediate called the **σ‑complex** (also known as the arenium ion). The reaction therefore proceeds faster – the group is *activating*.

Electron‑withdrawing groups (EWGs) such as –NO₂, –CF₃, –COOH, –SO₃H, and carbonyl‑containing groups pull electrons away from the ring. They make the σ‑complex less stable because the positive charge is less comfortably spread out. Consequently the ring reacts more slowly – the group is *deactivating*.

### Directing effects: where does the new substituent go?

When a substituent is already on the ring, it also tells the electrophile where to attach. The two main patterns are **ortho/para directing** and **meta directing**.  

- **Ortho** = the position next to the existing group (adjacent carbon).  
- **Meta** = the position one carbon away (separated by one carbon).  
- **Para** = the position opposite the existing group (across the ring).

#### Ortho/para directors (usually activating)

Most EDGs donate electron density to the ortho and para positions more than to the meta position. This happens because resonance structures that place the positive charge on the ortho or para carbon are especially stabilised. For example, the –OH group can be drawn as:

$$
\text{Ar–O}^- \leftrightarrow \text{Ar=O}^+
$$

The resonance forms show extra negative character at the ortho and para carbons, attracting the electrophile there. As a result, reactions with –OH, –OCH₃, –NH₂, alkyl groups, etc., give mainly ortho and para products.

#### Meta directors (usually deactivating)

EWGs withdraw electron density mainly by **inductive** effects or by resonance that places a positive charge on the carbon bearing the substituent. In the resonance forms, the ortho and para positions end up with a **positive** charge, which repels the incoming electrophile. The meta position, however, does not carry this extra positive charge, making it relatively more attractive. Therefore groups like –NO₂, –CF₃, –COOH, –SO₃H direct new substituents to the meta position.

> **Note:** Even though deactivating groups slow the overall reaction, they still guide the electrophile to the meta position; they do not stop the reaction completely.

### The role of Lewis acid catalysts

Many electrophiles are not strong enough on their own to attack the aromatic ring. A **Lewis acid** (a species that accepts an electron pair) can bind to the electrophile, increasing its positive character. Common Lewis acids in EAS are AlCl₃, FeCl₃, and BF₃.

For example, in the Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of benzene with an alkyl chloride, AlCl₃ coordinates to the chlorine atom:

$$
\text{R–Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{R}^+ \, \text{AlCl}_4^-
$$

The AlCl₃‑chloride complex pulls electron density away from the carbon‑chlorine bond, generating a carbocation‑like species **R⁺** that is a powerful electrophile. The aromatic ring then attacks this R⁺, completing the substitution.

Lewis acids also help in **Friedel‑Crafts acylation**, where an acyl chloride (R‑COCl) reacts with AlCl₃ to form an acylium ion **R‑C≡O⁺**, a very stable electrophile that adds to the ring and later loses a proton to restore aromaticity.

> **Remember:** The catalyst does not become part of the final product; it simply makes the electrophile more reactive and is regenerated at the end of the cycle.

### Putting it together

1. Look at the substituent already on the ring.  
2. Decide if it is electron‑donating (activating) or electron‑withdrawing (deactivating).  
3. Use its directing rule:  
   - Activating → ortho/para.  
   - Deactivating → meta.  
4. If the electrophile is weak, add a Lewis acid to boost its reactivity.  

By following these steps you can predict both **how fast** an EAS reaction will go and **where** the new group will appear on the aromatic ring. This systematic approach is a powerful tool for designing synthesis pathways in organic chemistry.

sections.heading: Practice Problems and Mechanism Drawing
sections.body:
**Guided Example – SN1 (Stepwise Substitution)**  

Imagine a bottle of soda that is sealed with a cork. First the cork pops off (the bond breaks), leaving a gap that other things can enter. In an SN1 reaction the carbon‑halogen bond breaks first, forming a *carbocation* (a positively‑charged carbon).  

Step 1 – **Leaving group departure**  
$$\text{R–Cl} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R}^{+} \;+\; \text{Cl}^{-}$$  
The chloride ion (Cl⁻) is the *leaving group*; it leaves because the solvent can stabilize the negative charge.  

Step 2 – **Nucleophile attack**  
The nucleophile (a species that “donates” an electron pair) rushes in and bonds to the carbocation:  
$$\text{R}^{+} \;+\; \text{Nu}^{-} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R–Nu}$$  

Because the carbocation is planar, the nucleophile can attack from either side, often giving a mixture of two mirror‑image products (racemic mixture).  

**Guided Example – SN2 (Concerted Substitution)**  

Think of a game of musical chairs where the nucleophile pushes the leaving group out of the seat in one smooth motion. In SN2 the bond to the leaving group breaks **while** the nucleophile forms a new bond – no intermediate is formed.  

Step 1 – **Single concerted step**  
$$\text{R–Cl} \;+\; \text{Nu}^{-} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R–Nu} \;+\; \text{Cl}^{-}$$  

The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group (the *back side*), leading to an inversion of the carbon’s geometry (like an umbrella turning inside‑out). This “one‑step” pathway works best when the carbon is not too crowded (primary or secondary).  

**Guided Example – Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS)**  

Picture a crowded round table (the aromatic ring). To add a new guest (an electrophile) we must first make a temporary seat by moving one of the existing guests (a π‑electron pair) onto the table’s edge.  

Step 1 – **Formation of the σ‑complex (arenium ion)**  
An electrophile (E⁺) attacks the ring, using one pair of π‑electrons:  
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \;+\; \text{E}^{+} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{–E}^{+}$$  

The ring now carries a positive charge (the σ‑complex).  

Step 2 – **Deprotonation (restoring aromaticity)**  
A base (often the solvent) removes a hydrogen atom from the carbon that just bonded to E⁺, returning the ring to its stable aromatic form:  
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{–E}^{+} \;+\; \text{Base} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{E} \;+\; \text{Base–H}^{+}$$  

The overall result is substitution of a hydrogen by the electrophile while the aromatic system stays intact.  

> **Note:** In SN1 the rate depends only on the substrate (first step), while in SN2 the rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile.  

> **Remember:** In EAS the aromatic ring never loses its aromaticity; the temporary σ‑complex quickly regains it by losing a proton.  

---

### Independent Practice  

1. **SN1 problem** – 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane reacts with water.  
   a) Write the two‑step mechanism.  
   b) Predict the major product(s).  

2. **SN2 problem** – Chloromethane reacts with hydroxide ion (OH⁻).  
   a) Draw the single concerted step.  
   b) Indicate the stereochemical outcome.  

3. **EAS problem** – Nitration of benzene using HNO₃/H₂SO₄.  
   a) Show the electrophile formed.  
   b) Outline the two steps of substitution.  
   c) What is the product?  

### Answer Key  

1. a) Step 1: (CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻  
   Step 2: (CH₃)₃C⁺ + H₂O → (CH₃)₃C–OH₂⁺ → (CH₃)₃C–OH + H⁺  
   b) Tertiary alcohol **tert‑butanol** is the major product; a small amount of rearranged product is unlikely because the carbocation is already stable.  

2. a) $$\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{Cl}^{-}$$  
   b) No stereochemistry issue for CH₃Cl (no chiral center), but the reaction proceeds with inversion if a chiral center were present.  

3. a) The strong acid mixture generates the nitronium ion: $$\text{NO}_2^{+}$$  
   b) Step 1: Benzene + NO₂⁺ → σ‑complex (arenium ion).  
      Step 2: Base (HSO₄⁻) removes a proton → nitrobenzene + H₂SO₄.  
   c) **Nitrobenzene** is the final product.

examples.title: SN1 of tert‑butyl chloride in water
examples.given: tert‑butyl chloride (CH₃)₃CCl reacts with water; identify the mechanism and the major product.

steps.label: Identify substrate
steps.text: Tertiary carbon attached to Cl → good for SN1 because carbocation is stable.

steps.label: Form carbocation
steps.text: Cl leaves, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺; leaving group ability of Cl⁻ is sufficient in polar protic water.

steps.label: Nucleophilic attack
steps.text: Water attacks the carbocation, giving (CH₃)₃C–OH₂⁺.

steps.label: Deprotonate
steps.text: Another water molecule removes a proton, yielding tert‑butanol ((CH₃)₃COH).

examples.answer: The reaction proceeds by an SN1 mechanism and the major product is tert‑butanol, (CH₃)₃COH.

examples.title: SN2 of 1‑bromopropane with NaCN in DMSO
examples.given: 1‑bromopropane (CH₃CH₂CH₂Br) reacts with NaCN in dimethyl sulfoxide; determine the mechanism, stereochemistry, and product.

steps.label: Assess substrate
steps.text: Primary alkyl halide → favors SN2 because steric hindrance is low.

steps.label: Check solvent
steps.text: DMSO is polar aprotic, which stabilizes the nucleophile (CN⁻) and enhances SN2 rates.

steps.label: Nucleophilic attack
steps.text: CN⁻ attacks the carbon bearing Br from the backside, forming a transition state with simultaneous bond making and breaking.

steps.label: Invert configuration
steps.text: The carbon is achiral here, but the backside attack leads to inversion of configuration if a chiral center were present.

steps.label: Release leaving group
steps.text: Br⁻ departs, giving propionitrile (CH₃CH₂CH₂CN).

examples.answer: The reaction follows an SN2 pathway; the product is propionitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂CN, with backside attack and inversion of configuration.

examples.title: Electrophilic aromatic substitution of anisole with bromine (Br₂) in FeBr₃; predict major product and orientation.
examples.given: Anisole (methoxybenzene) is treated with Br₂/FeBr₃; decide which position the bromine adds to and name the product.

steps.label: Identify activating group
steps.text: The –OCH₃ group is an electron‑donating resonance activator, making the ring more reactive toward EAS.

steps.label: Determine directing effects
steps.text: –OCH₃ is ortho/para directing because its lone pair can donate into the ring, stabilizing carbocation intermediates at those positions.

steps.label: Evaluate steric factors
steps.text: Ortho positions are sterically hindered by the –OCH₃ group; para position is less hindered.

steps.label: Form σ‑complex
steps.text: Attack of Br⁺ (generated by FeBr₃) at the para position gives the most stable σ‑complex (para‑bromination).

steps.label: Deprotonate
steps.text: Loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity, yielding para‑bromoanisole.

examples.answer: Bromination occurs mainly at the para position; the major product is para‑bromoanisole (4‑bromo‑anisole).

practice.q: Which of the following is a good nucleophile in an SN2 reaction: I⁻, H₂O, CH₃CH₂OH, or NH₃? Explain why.
practice.a: I⁻ is the best nucleophile. Nucleophilicity in SN2 reactions increases with charge and basicity. I⁻ is negatively charged, has a large, polarizable electron cloud, and is not strongly solvated in polar aprotic solvents, making it very reactive toward electrophilic carbon. H₂O and CH₃CH₂OH are neutral and hydrogen‑bonded, so they are weaker nucleophiles. NH₃ is neutral and less polarizable than I⁻, so it is also weaker.

practice.q: Predict the major product when 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane reacts with water (H₂O) under warm conditions. Show the mechanism briefly.
practice.a:
2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane (tert‑butyl bromide) undergoes an SN1 reaction with water.
1. **Step 1 – Formation of carbocation:** The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, giving a tertiary carbocation (tert‑butyl⁺) and Br⁻.
2. **Step 2 – Nucleophilic attack:** Water attacks the carbocation, forming an oxonium ion (tert‑butyl‑OH₂⁺).
3. **Step 3 – Deprotonation:** Another water molecule removes a proton, giving tert‑butanol (2‑methyl‑2‑propanol) as the major product.
Thus, the product is tert‑butanol.

practice.q: For the reaction of 1‑bromobutane with NaOH in ethanol, determine whether the mechanism is SN1 or SN2 and justify your answer. Draw the mechanism showing all intermediates.
practice.a:
1‑bromobutane is a primary alkyl halide. Primary substrates favor SN2 because:
- The carbon bearing the leaving group is only attached to one other carbon, giving little steric hindrance.
- SN1 requires a stable carbocation, which a primary carbocation cannot provide.
Therefore, the reaction proceeds by SN2.
**Mechanism:**
1. **Nucleophilic attack:** OH⁻ (from NaOH) attacks the carbon bearing Br from the backside, forming a transition state where the C–Br bond is breaking and the C–O bond is forming.
2. **Leaving group departure:** The C–Br bond fully breaks, releasing Br⁻.
3. **Product:** n‑butanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH) is formed with inversion of configuration at the carbon (though the carbon is achiral here). No intermediates are isolated; only a single transition state exists.

practice.q: Explain why chlorobenzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) slower than benzene. Include the role of resonance and inductive effects.
practice.a:
In EAS, the aromatic ring attacks an electrophile, forming a σ‑complex (Wheland intermediate). For chlorobenzene:
- **Inductive effect (–I):** Chlorine is electronegative and withdraws electron density through the σ‑bond framework, making the ring less nucleophilic.
- **Resonance effect (+R):** Chlorine can donate a lone pair into the ring, but this donation occurs mainly at the ortho and para positions and does not fully compensate for the –I effect in the transition state.
- In the σ‑complex, the positive charge is delocalized onto the carbon bearing chlorine, where chlorine’s –I effect destabilizes the intermediate.
Thus, the overall activation energy for chlorobenzene is higher, and the reaction proceeds more slowly than with benzene, which lacks any electron‑withdrawing substituent.

practice.q: Predict the major product(s) and stereochemistry when (R)-2‑bromo‑3‑methylbutane reacts with a excess of NaCN in DMSO. Show the mechanism and explain why any side reactions are minimal.
practice.a:
(R)-2‑bromo‑3‑methylbutane is a secondary bromide. In DMSO (polar aprotic), NaCN provides the strong nucleophile CN⁻, favoring SN2.
**Mechanism:**
1. **Back‑side attack:** CN⁻ attacks the carbon bearing Br from the side opposite the leaving group, forming a transition state where the C–Br bond is breaking and the C–CN bond is forming.
2. **Inversion of configuration:** Because the attack is backside, the stereocenter inverts from (R) to (S).
3. **Product:** (S)-2‑cyanobutane‑3‑methyl (i.e., (S)-2‑cyanopentane). No carbocation forms, so rearrangements or elimination (E2) are minimal; the polar aprotic solvent stabilizes the nucleophile but not the leaving group, suppressing side reactions.
Thus, the major product is the (S)-nitrile with complete inversion of configuration.

practice.q: A nitration reaction is carried out on anisole (methoxybenzene) using a mixture of concentrated H₂SO₄ and HNO₃. (a) Predict the major regioisomer(s) formed and justify the orientation. (b) Propose a detailed step‑by‑step mechanism for the formation of the major product, including the formation of the nitronium ion.
practice.a:
(a) **Regioselectivity:** The methoxy group is a strong +R (electron‑donating) group. It activates the ortho and para positions and deactivates the meta position. Therefore, nitration of anisole gives mainly ortho‑ and para‑nitroanisole, with the para product being predominant due to steric hindrance at the ortho positions.
(b) **Mechanism:**
1. **Generation of the electrophile (nitronium ion):**
H₂SO₄ + HNO₃ ⇌ H₂NO₃⁺ + HSO₄⁻
H₂NO₃⁺ → NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion) + H₂O
2. **Attack of the aromatic ring:** The π‑electrons of the anisole ring at the ortho or para position attack the NO₂⁺, forming a σ‑complex (Wheland intermediate) where the positive charge is delocalized onto the ring and especially onto the carbon bearing the methoxy group.
3. **Resonance stabilization:** The methoxy oxygen donates electron density by resonance, stabilizing the positive charge in the intermediate, especially when the electrophile is at the para position.
4. **Deprotonation:** A base (HSO₄⁻ or H₂O) removes the proton from the carbon that added the electrophile, restoring aromaticity and yielding para‑nitroanisole as the major product. Minor ortho‑nitroanisole is also formed.

data.recap: This lesson introduces substitution reactions in organic chemistry, focusing on nucleophiles, electrophiles, and leaving groups. It explains the two main mechanisms, SN1 (stepwise, forming a carbocation) and SN2 (single‑step, backside attack), and compares their requirements and outcomes. The section on electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) shows how aromatic rings act as nucleophiles and how substituents influence reactivity and orientation.
