lessons.title: Key Organic Reactions II: Addition and Elimination
lessons.focus: Cover addition to alkenes/alkynes, elimination (E1, E2), and factors influencing each.

data.title: Key Organic Reactions II: Addition and Elimination
data.summary: This lesson explains how addition reactions add atoms to double or triple bonds and how elimination reactions remove atoms to form double bonds. It also examines the factors that control whether a reaction follows an addition, E1, or E2 pathway.
objectives: Identify the difference between addition and elimination reactions
Predict the product of a simple alkene or alkyne addition
Distinguish between E1 and E2 mechanisms and write their stepwise arrows
Explain how substrate structure, base strength, and solvent affect reaction pathways
Apply the concepts to choose appropriate conditions for a given organic transformation
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic functional groups, bond polarity, and the idea of reaction mechanisms from earlier lessons.
why: Addition and elimination reactions are the workhorses of organic synthesis. They allow chemists to build larger molecules or create functional groups needed for medicines, plastics, and fuels.
Knowing which conditions favor addition versus elimination helps students design efficient laboratory procedures and understand how nature builds complex molecules in metabolism.

sections.heading: 1. Review of Alkenes and Alkynes
sections.body:
Alkenes and alkynes are the simplest members of the family of **unsaturated** hydrocarbons.  
The word *unsaturated* means that the carbon atoms do not have the maximum number of single (σ) bonds possible; instead they share extra electrons in **π (pi) bonds**.  

> **Definition:** A **π bond** is formed when two parallel p‑orbitals on adjacent atoms overlap side‑by‑side. It sits above and below the plane of the σ bond that holds the two atoms together.

In an alkene the carbon‑carbon double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond:

$$\text{C=C} \;=\; \sigma + \pi$$  

In an alkyne the carbon‑carbon triple bond contains one σ bond and **two** π bonds:

$$\text{C≡C} \;=\; \sigma + 2\pi$$  

Because π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of p‑orbitals, they are **weaker** and **more exposed** than σ bonds. The electron cloud of a π bond sits above and below the line joining the two carbon nuclei, making it easier for other molecules to approach and interact with those electrons.

> **Note:** The σ bond is the strongest bond in a carbon‑carbon link; it holds the two carbons together. The π bond is the “extra” bond that gives the molecule its reactivity.

### Why π Bonds Are Reactive

Think of a double‑door entrance. The main door (σ bond) is solid and hard to open, while the side doors (π bonds) are lighter and swing outward. A passer‑by can more easily push the side doors open. In chemistry, a **nucleophile** (electron‑rich species) or an **electrophile** (electron‑poor species) can interact with the π electrons because they are more accessible. When this happens, the π bond is broken and new σ bonds are formed – this is the essence of an **addition reaction**.

### Visualising the Geometry

- In an alkene, each carbon of the C=C bond is **sp² hybridised**. This means three hybrid orbitals lie in a plane at 120° angles, and the remaining p‑orbital (which makes the π bond) points perpendicular to that plane.
- In an alkyne, each carbon is **sp hybridised**. Two hybrid orbitals line up in a straight line (180°), and two p‑orbitals remain perpendicular to each other, creating the two π bonds.

> **In daily life:** The shape of an alkyne (a straight line) is why compounds like acetylene are used in welding torches – the linear geometry lets the flame focus into a narrow, high‑energy beam.

### Consequences for Reactivity

1. **Alkenes** react faster than alkynes in many addition reactions because they have only one π bond to break.  
2. **Alkynes** can undergo two successive additions (first converting the triple bond to a double bond, then to a single bond) because they have two π bonds.  
3. The **strength** of the π bond influences how much energy is needed to start the reaction. A typical C=C π bond energy is about 65 kcal mol⁻¹, while a single C≡C π bond is about 45 kcal mol⁻¹; the extra π bond in an alkyne makes it slightly less stable overall.

### Simple Example

Consider ethene, the simplest alkene:

$$\text{CH}_2= \text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_3$$  

Hydrogen (H₂) adds across the double bond. The π electrons of the C=C bond attack the H–H bond, breaking the π bond and forming two new C–H σ bonds. The result is ethane, a saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds.

### Key Take‑aways

- **π bonds are the reactive sites** in alkenes and alkynes because they are weaker and more exposed than σ bonds.  
- The geometry (sp² vs. sp) tells us the shape of the molecule and helps predict how it will interact with other chemicals.  
- Understanding the nature of these bonds prepares us to follow the step‑by‑step mechanisms of addition and elimination reactions that come later in the lesson.

> **Remember:** Whenever you see a double or triple bond, think “π bond ready to be added to.” This mental picture will guide you through the many reactions we will study next.

sections.heading: 2. General Concept of Addition Reactions
sections.body:
Addition reactions are a way for molecules that contain a double or triple bond to **gain** new atoms.  
Think of a double bond as a “two‑lane highway” that can let two cars (the two carbon atoms) travel side‑by‑side. When a new car (an atom or a group of atoms) wants to join the traffic, the highway must narrow to a single lane so that the new car can fit. In chemistry this means the π (pi) bond of the double or triple bond is broken and two new σ (sigma) bonds are formed with the incoming atoms.

> **Definition:** An addition reaction is a chemical process in which a molecule with a multiple bond (C=C or C≡C) reacts with another species, converting the π bond into two new σ bonds and increasing the total number of atoms attached to the carbon skeleton.

Why does this happen?  
The π bond is formed from the sideways overlap of p‑orbitals. This overlap is weaker than the head‑on overlap that makes a σ bond. Because the π bond is weaker, it is easier for another reagent to attack the carbon atoms and break the π bond. The result is a more stable molecule with only σ bonds, which are the strongest type of covalent bond.

> **Note:** σ bonds are stronger than π bonds because the electron density lies directly between the two nuclei, giving a tighter, lower‑energy connection.

### Electrophilic addition – the most common type

The most frequent addition reactions are **electrophilic additions**. The word *electrophilic* means “electron‑loving”. An electrophile is a species that is deficient in electrons and therefore seeks out a place rich in electrons. The double bond is a good electron donor because the π electrons are loosely held and can be shared.

A classic, simple example is the addition of hydrogen bromide (HBr) to ethene (CH₂=CH₂).

1. **Step 1 – Attack of the electrophile**  
   The H atom in HBr carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺) because bromine is more electronegative and pulls electron density toward itself. This makes H⁺ an electrophile. The π electrons of the C=C bond jump onto one of the carbon atoms, forming a new σ bond between that carbon and H⁺.

2. **Step 2 – Capture of the nucleophile**  
   After the H⁺ is attached, the bromide ion (Br⁻) is left behind. Br⁻ is a *nucleophile* (electron‑rich species) and quickly bonds to the positively charged carbon that did not receive the hydrogen. The result is a saturated molecule: bromoethane.

The overall change can be written as  

$$\text{CH}_2= \text{CH}_2 \;+\; \text{HBr} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{CH}_3\!-\!\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$$  

Notice that the double bond (one π bond) disappears and two new σ bonds appear: a C–H bond and a C–Br bond.

> **In daily life:** Adding HBr to ethene is similar to adding a new piece to a broken puzzle. The broken edge (the π bond) is replaced by two new pieces (the C–H and C–Br bonds) that fit snugly together, completing the picture.

### Why electrophilic addition is useful

- **Creates functional groups:** By choosing different electrophiles (HCl, H₂O, H₂SO₄, etc.) we can introduce chlorine, hydroxyl, or sulfonate groups into a molecule, changing its chemical behavior.
- **Builds complexity:** Many larger organic molecules are assembled step‑by‑step from simple alkenes using addition reactions.
- **Predictable regio‑selectivity:** In unsymmetrical alkenes, the electrophile usually adds to the carbon that can form the more stable carbocation intermediate (the *Markovnikov rule*). This predictability helps chemists design synthesis routes.

> **Remember:** In an electrophilic addition, the π bond supplies electrons to an electrophile, forming a new σ bond, and the leftover nucleophile finishes the reaction by bonding to the other carbon.

### Quick checklist for recognizing an addition reaction

- Starts with a molecule that has a double or triple bond.  
- Ends with a molecule where that multiple bond is gone and two new single bonds have formed.  
- Often involves an electrophile (electron‑poor) and a nucleophile (electron‑rich).  

Understanding this general concept will make the detailed mechanisms (like the step‑by‑step arrows you will see later) much easier to follow.

sections.heading: 3. Mechanism of Electrophilic Addition to Alkenes
sections.body:
When an alkene meets a reagent that wants electrons, the double bond acts like a “hand‑shake” partner. The double bond is a region of high electron density, so it can donate a pair of electrons to an electrophile (a species that is electron‑poor). This first step creates a positively charged carbon atom, called a **carbocation**, and attaches the electrophile to the other carbon of the double bond.

> **Definition:** *Electrophilic addition* – a reaction in which an electrophile adds to a carbon–carbon multiple bond, followed by attack of a nucleophile on the resulting carbocation.

---

### Step 1 – The electrophile attacks

Take the classic example of adding hydrogen bromide (HBr) to ethene (CH₂=CH₂). The H–Br bond is polarized: hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺) because bromine is more electronegative, while bromine carries a partial negative charge (δ⁻). The alkene’s π electrons (the electrons of the double bond) are attracted to the δ⁺ hydrogen.

```
   Hδ⁺—Brδ⁻   +   CH2=CH2   →   [CH3–CH2⁺]   +   Br⁻
```

The curved arrow starts at the π bond and ends at the hydrogen atom, showing that the electrons are used to form a new C–H σ bond. As a result, the hydrogen attaches to one carbon, and the other carbon is left with only three bonds – it becomes a carbocation.

> **Note:** The carbon that receives the hydrogen becomes positively charged because it now has only six electrons in its valence shell (four from its own bonds plus two from the new C–H bond).

### Step 2 – Nucleophilic attack

The bromide ion (Br⁻) that was released in the first step is a **nucleophile** – a species that loves to donate electrons. It is attracted to the positively charged carbon and uses its lone pair to form a new C–Br bond.

```
   Br⁻   +   CH3–CH2⁺   →   CH3–CH2–Br
```

The arrow goes from the lone pair on Br⁻ to the carbocation, completing the addition. The final product is bromoethane, and the original double bond is gone.

> **Remember:** The overall reaction is the sum of the two arrow‑pushing steps; no extra atoms appear or disappear.

### Regioselectivity – Where does the electrophile add?

If the alkene is unsymmetrical, such as propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂), two different carbocations can form:

1. **Markovnikov addition** – the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens (the “less substituted” carbon). This leaves the positively charged carbon on the more substituted side (the carbon attached to the CH₃ group). More substituted carbocations are more stable because they are better at spreading out the positive charge.

2. **Anti‑Markovnikov addition** – the hydrogen adds to the more substituted carbon, putting the positive charge on the less substituted carbon. This pathway is less common for HBr, but it becomes dominant when a peroxide (ROOR) is present, because a radical mechanism changes the order of steps.

The rule can be remembered with the phrase “the rich get richer”: the carbon that can stabilize the positive charge best (the more substituted one) ends up bearing the charge, and the electrophile adds to the opposite carbon.

$$\text{Markovnikov: } \text{H adds to the less substituted carbon, } \text{X adds to the more substituted carbon}$$  
$$\text{Anti‑Markovnikov: } \text{H adds to the more substituted carbon, } \text{X adds to the less substituted carbon}$$

> **In daily life:** Think of a crowded bus stop. People (electrons) prefer to stand where there is more room (a more substituted carbon can “hold” the positive charge better). The first person (hydrogen) goes to the less crowded spot, leaving the crowded spot for the next arrival (the nucleophile).

### Why the mechanism matters

Understanding each arrow tells you where new bonds will form and which products are favored. This helps chemists design syntheses: by choosing the right reagent and conditions, they can direct the addition to give the desired isomer. For example, using peroxide to force anti‑Markovnikov addition lets you make a primary alkyl bromide from an alkene that would otherwise give a secondary bromide.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming the electrophile always adds to the carbon with more hydrogens. Remember the stability of the intermediate carbocation dictates the outcome, not the number of hydrogens on the carbon that initially receives the electrophile.

sections.heading: 4. Addition to Alkynes
sections.body:
Alkynes are carbon‑carbon triple‑bonded molecules.  
The triple bond is made of one σ (sigma) bond and two π (pi) bonds.  
The σ bond is strong and holds the two carbon atoms together, while the two π bonds are weaker and sit above and below the line of the σ bond. Because there are **two** π bonds, an alkyne has **two places where other atoms can add**.

> **Definition:** An *addition reaction* is a chemical process in which two or more small molecules combine to form a larger one, usually by breaking a π bond and forming new σ bonds.

When a reagent approaches an alkyne, it first attacks one of the π bonds. After the first addition, the alkyne becomes an *alkene* (a double bond). The remaining π bond can then react a second time, giving a *single‑bonded* product. Whether the reaction stops after the first addition or goes on to the second depends on the reagent, the reaction conditions, and the stability of the intermediate formed.

### First addition: water + acid (hydration)

Consider the classic hydration of an alkyne using water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$) in the presence of a strong acid (often $\mathrm{H^+}$ from sulfuric acid). The overall transformation is:

$$\ce{RC#CR' + H2O -> RCOH-CH2R'}$$

1. **Protonation** – The acid donates a proton ($\mathrm{H^+}$) to one carbon of the triple bond, creating a *carbocation* (a positively charged carbon).  
   $$\ce{RC#CR' + H+ -> RC^+–C=R'}$$  
   The positive charge prefers the more substituted carbon because that carbocation is more stable (it is surrounded by more carbon groups that can donate electron density).

2. **Nucleophilic attack** – Water, acting as a *nucleophile* (a species that donates an electron pair), attacks the carbocation, forming an *enol* (a molecule with a carbon‑oxygen double bond next to a carbon‑carbon double bond).  
   $$\ce{RC^+–C=R' + H2O -> RC(OH)=CH–R'}$$

3. **Tautomerization** – The enol quickly rearranges to a more stable *ketone* or *aldehyde* (a carbonyl compound) by moving a hydrogen atom and shifting the double bond.  
   $$\ce{RC(OH)=CH–R' -> RC(=O)CH2R'}$$

Only **one** addition occurs here because the product is a carbonyl compound, which is much less reactive toward further addition under the same acidic conditions. The carbonyl carbon is already fully saturated with four bonds, so the reaction stops.

### Second addition: halogen (e.g., Br₂)

When a halogen such as bromine ($\ce{Br2}$) is added to an alkyne, the reaction can happen **twice**, giving a *tetra‑halogenated* alkane.

First addition:

1. **Formation of a cyclic bromonium ion** – One bromine atom attaches to the alkyne, forming a three‑membered ring where the bromine carries a positive charge.  
   $$\ce{RC#CR' + Br2 -> [RC(Br)–C(Br)R']^+}$$

2. **Ring opening** – The other bromide ion ($\ce{Br-}$) attacks the more substituted carbon of the ring, opening it and giving a *dibromoalkene* (a double bond with one bromine on each carbon).  
   $$\ce{[RC(Br)–C(Br)R']^+ + Br- -> RC(Br)=C(Br)R'}$$

Second addition:

The newly formed double bond is still a π bond, so a second molecule of $\ce{Br2}$ can add in the same way, producing a *tetrabromoalkane* (all single bonds).  

$$\ce{RC(Br)=C(Br)R' + Br2 -> RC(Br)–C(Br)–C(Br)–C(Br)R'}$$

> **Note:** The first addition to an alkyne creates a double bond, which is still reactive. If excess halogen is present, a second addition is common, giving a fully saturated product.

### Why does the second addition sometimes not happen?

- **Reaction conditions:** In acidic hydration, the carbonyl product is not a good target for another water molecule under the same conditions.  
- **Reagent amount:** If only a stoichiometric amount of $\ce{H2O/H+}$ is used, there is no extra electrophile to attack the new double bond.  
- **Stability of intermediate:** The enol formed after the first addition quickly tautomerizes to a carbonyl, which is much less nucleophilic than an alkene.

> **In daily life:** Think of a triple‑bonded alkyne like a two‑lane highway. The first car (reagent) can use one lane, turning the highway into a two‑lane road (an alkene). If traffic continues (more reagent), a second car can use the remaining lane, turning the road into a one‑lane street (a single bond). If the road is closed after the first car (as with a carbonyl), no more cars can pass.

> **Remember:** An alkyne can undergo *one* addition to become an alkene, and *two* additions to become a saturated molecule. The number of additions depends on the reagent, its amount, and how stable the intermediate product is.

sections.heading: 5. Introduction to Elimination Reactions
sections.body:
When we talk about **elimination reactions**, we are looking at a process that does the opposite of what we saw in addition reactions.  

In an addition reaction a molecule **adds** to a double or triple bond, turning an alkene or alkyne into a more saturated compound. In an elimination reaction a single molecule **leaves** (or is removed) from a saturated carbon chain, and a new double bond is created in its place.  

> **Definition:** An elimination reaction is a chemical transformation in which a substrate loses a small fragment (called a *leaving group*) and, at the same time, a new π‑bond (a double bond) forms between two adjacent carbon atoms.  

The overall change can be written very simply:

$$\text{substrate} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{alkene} + \text{leaving group}$$  

Here “substrate” means the original molecule that contains a carbon–hydrogen (C–H) bond and a carbon–leaving‑group (C–LG) bond on neighboring carbons. The “leaving group” is the part that departs; common leaving groups are halides (Cl⁻, Br⁻), tosylates, or water (when a –OH group is first turned into a good leaving group).  

### Why does elimination happen?

Think of a crowded hallway. If two people are standing side‑by‑side, they can’t move forward because they block each other. If one of them steps out of the hallway, the other can now walk straight ahead. In a molecule, the two carbon atoms are “blocked” by the atoms attached to them. When a leaving group steps away, the two carbons are free to form a double bond, allowing the molecule to become more stable under the right conditions (usually heat or a base).

### Everyday comparison

Imagine a pair of shoes tied together with a short rope. The rope keeps the shoes close, preventing them from spreading apart. If you cut the rope, the shoes can slide apart and the space between them widens. In elimination chemistry, the “rope” is the bond to the leaving group; cutting it (removing the group) lets the two carbon atoms move closer together and share a double bond.

### Step‑by‑step picture of what is happening

1. **Identify the leaving group.** This is the atom or group that can depart easily, often because it can stabilize the negative charge it takes with it (e.g., Cl⁻).  
2. **Identify a hydrogen atom on the adjacent carbon.** This hydrogen will be taken away together with the leaving group.  
3. **Form the double bond.** When the leaving group leaves and the hydrogen is removed, the two carbons share a pair of electrons, creating a π‑bond (the double bond).  
4. **Result:** The original saturated carbon skeleton is now an *alkene* (a molecule with a carbon–carbon double bond), and the leaving group is released as a separate ion or molecule.

> **Note:** Elimination reactions usually need either heat or a strong base (a substance that likes to take protons). Heat supplies the energy to break bonds, while a base helps pull off the hydrogen atom.

### When does elimination compete with addition?

In many reactions, especially those involving alkyl halides, both addition and elimination are possible. The direction the reaction takes depends on conditions:

- **Cold, polar solvents** and a nucleophile favor addition because the nucleophile can quickly attack the double bond.  
- **Hot conditions** or a strong base favor elimination because the extra energy or the base’s ability to pull off a hydrogen makes the leaving‑group departure easier.

> **Remember:** If you see a reaction carried out at high temperature with a strong base like NaOH or KOH, think “elimination is likely”.

### A simple example

Consider 2‑bromo‑butane (CH₃‑CH(Br)‑CH₂‑CH₃). When it is treated with a strong base such as potassium tert‑butoxide (KOtBu) and heated, the base removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the carbon bearing the bromine. Simultaneously, the bromide ion (Br⁻) leaves. The product is but‑2‑ene (CH₃‑CH=CH‑CH₃) plus Br⁻.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \;\xrightarrow{\text{KOtBu, heat}}\; \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3 + \text{Br}^-$$  

The reaction removed a small fragment (Br⁻) and created a double bond between the two middle carbons.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the hydrogen removed must be on the carbon *adjacent* to the leaving group. If the hydrogen is farther away, the reaction cannot form the required double bond in a single step.

### Key take‑aways

- Elimination removes a leaving group and a hydrogen from neighboring carbons, forming a double bond.  
- It is driven by heat or a strong base, which helps break the bonds.  
- The result is an alkene plus a separate leaving group.  

Understanding elimination gives you a powerful tool to predict how organic molecules change under different conditions, and it sets the stage for learning the two main mechanisms, E1 and E2, that we will explore next.

sections.heading: 6. E1 Mechanism
sections.body:
The E1 reaction is a **two‑step** way that a molecule loses a small piece (usually a hydrogen halide, HX) and forms a double bond.  
Think of it like a two‑stage dance: first the partner steps away, leaving an open spot, then another partner steps in to finish the move.

**Step 1 – Carbocation formation**  
When a substrate such as a secondary or tertiary alkyl halide is placed in a polar protic solvent (for example, water or alcohol), the bond between carbon and the leaving group (the halogen) breaks. The halogen takes both electrons from the bond and leaves as a negatively charged ion (X⁻). The carbon that was attached to the halogen is left without its full complement of electrons, so it becomes a positively charged carbon called a **carbocation**.

> **Definition:** A *carbocation* is a carbon atom that carries a positive charge because it has only six valence electrons instead of the usual eight.

The solvent helps this step because its molecules can surround and stabilize the charged pieces (the halide ion and the carbocation) through hydrogen‑bonding and dipole interactions. This stabilization lowers the energy needed to break the C–X bond.

**Step 2 – Deprotonation**  
In the second step a weak base (often the solvent itself, such as water or an alcohol) removes a hydrogen atom from a carbon atom that is adjacent to the carbocation. When the hydrogen (as a proton, H⁺) leaves, the electrons from the C–H bond move to form a new π‑bond (a double bond) between the two carbons. The result is an alkene and the conjugate acid of the base (for example, H₃O⁺ if water was the base).

$$\text{R–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–X} \;\xrightarrow{\text{polar protic}} \;\text{R–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2^{+} \;+\; \text{X}^- \;\xrightarrow{\text{weak base}} \;\text{R–CH}= \text{CH}_2 \;+\; \text{HB}^+$$

> **Note:** The base in an E1 reaction is *weak*; it does not have to pull the proton away quickly. The reaction rate is controlled mainly by how easily the carbocation forms, not by how fast the base acts.

### Why carbocation stability matters  

Not all carbocations are created equal. A carbocation that is more stable will form more readily, making the overall E1 reaction faster. Stability follows these trends:

1. **Tertiary > secondary > primary** – More alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon donate electron density (through hyper‑conjugation and inductive effects), spreading out the positive charge.
2. **Allylic and benzylic carbocations** are especially stable because the positive charge can be shared with a neighboring double bond or aromatic ring (resonance stabilization).
3. **Ring strain** and **electron‑withdrawing groups** destabilize a carbocation, slowing the reaction.

Because the first step is the slow, rate‑determining step, chemists often look at the substrate’s ability to form a stable carbocation when deciding whether an elimination will follow an E1 pathway.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a crowded hallway where a person (the leaving group) steps out of the line, creating an empty spot. If the surrounding people (alkyl groups) are friendly and can quickly fill the gap, the line moves smoothly. If the surrounding people are few or unfriendly, the gap stays open longer, and the whole process slows down.

### Typical conditions for an E1 reaction  

| Condition | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| **Polar protic solvent** (e.g., water, ethanol) | Stabilizes ions through hydrogen bonding, lowering the energy of the carbocation and the leaving group. |
| **Weak base** (e.g., water, alcohol) | Does not compete with the leaving group for the carbon; it only removes a proton after the carbocation is formed. |
| **Heat** (often 50–100 °C) | Provides the extra energy needed to break the C–X bond and to overcome the activation barrier for carbocation formation. |
| **Tertiary or secondary alkyl halide** | These substrates can generate relatively stable carbocations. |

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that a strong base will always give an E1 reaction. In fact, a strong base usually pushes the reaction toward an E2 mechanism, where bond breaking and making happen in a single concerted step.

### Putting it together  

1. **Identify** a substrate that can form a stable carbocation (tertiary, allylic, benzylic).  
2. **Choose** a polar protic solvent and a weak base.  
3. **Heat** the mixture gently.  
4. **Watch** the leaving group depart, creating the carbocation.  
5. **Allow** the solvent (or another weak base) to pull off a neighboring hydrogen, forming the double bond.

When you follow these steps, the molecule undergoes an E1 elimination, turning a saturated carbon chain into an unsaturated alkene. Understanding the role of carbocation stability helps you predict when this pathway will dominate over other possibilities, such as substitution (SN1) or the concerted E2 elimination.

sections.heading: 7. E2 Mechanism
sections.body:
When we talk about an **E2 reaction**, we mean a *single‑step* process that turns a carbon‑hydrogen (C–H) bond and a carbon‑halogen (C–X) bond into a new carbon‑carbon double bond (C=C). The “E” stands for elimination, and the “2” tells us that two atoms (the hydrogen and the halogen) leave at the same time.

> **Definition:** An **E2 mechanism** is a concerted, one‑step elimination where a strong base removes a β‑hydrogen while the leaving group departs, forming a double bond in a single, synchronized motion.

### The basic picture

Imagine a pair of hands holding a rope. One hand pulls the rope tight (the base taking the hydrogen), while the other hand lets go of the knot (the leaving group leaving). Both actions happen together; there is no pause where the rope is loose. In chemistry, the “hands” are the base and the leaving group, and the “rope” is the carbon skeleton that becomes a double bond.

### Why a strong base is needed

A base is a molecule that likes to grab a proton (H⁺). In an E2 reaction the base must be strong enough to pull the hydrogen off **while** the carbon‑halogen bond is breaking. If the base is weak, it cannot compete with other possible pathways (like substitution), and the reaction will be slow or may not happen at all.

> **Note:** Typical strong bases are hydroxide (OH⁻), alkoxides (RO⁻), or amide (NH₂⁻). They have high affinity for protons and are good at “snatching” the β‑hydrogen in the same instant the leaving group leaves.

### Antiperiplanar geometry – the right alignment

For the simultaneous pull‑and‑let‑go to work efficiently, the hydrogen that is being removed (the β‑hydrogen) and the leaving group (the halogen, X) must be positioned **antiperiplanar**. This means they lie on opposite sides of the carbon‑carbon bond and are roughly 180° apart, like two opposite seats on a seesaw.

Why does this matter? In the transition state—the fleeting arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy hill—the orbitals that form the new double bond must line up. When the H and X are antiperiplanar, their orbitals can overlap cleanly, allowing the electrons from the C–H bond to flow into the forming C=C bond while the electrons in the C–X bond go to the leaving group.

If the required antiperiplanar arrangement is impossible because of the molecule’s shape, the E2 reaction will be much slower or may not occur at all.

> **Remember:** Look for a β‑hydrogen that is antiperiplanar to the leaving group; if you can’t find one, the E2 pathway is disfavored.

### How substrate structure influences the rate

1. **Primary, secondary, tertiary carbon attached to the leaving group**  
   - **Primary** (attached to only one other carbon) substrates react fastest in E2 because steric hindrance is low; the base can approach the β‑hydrogen easily.  
   - **Secondary** substrates are slower but still react well if a good antiperiplanar hydrogen is present.  
   - **Tertiary** substrates are the slowest for E2 because the bulky groups block the base’s access to the β‑hydrogen. In such cases, the reaction often switches to an E1 mechanism instead.

2. **Leaving group ability**  
   A good leaving group (e.g., I⁻, Br⁻, tosylate) departs readily, lowering the energy needed for the transition state. Poor leaving groups (e.g., OH⁻) make the E2 step much harder.

3. **Base strength and size**  
   Small, strong bases (like NaOCH₃) can reach crowded β‑hydrogens more easily than bulky bases (like KOtBu). Bulky bases tend to favor elimination over substitution because they cannot fit into the carbon atom to perform a substitution.

4. **Conformation of the substrate**  
   In cyclic compounds, the ring forces certain bonds into fixed positions. An E2 reaction will only occur if the β‑hydrogen and leaving group can adopt the antiperiplanar geometry within the ring. For example, in cyclohexane derivatives, the axial‑axial arrangement provides the needed geometry, while an equatorial‑equatorial pair does not.

### Putting it together – the overall equation

The generic E2 reaction can be written as:

$$
\text{R–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–X} + \text{Base}^- \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R–CH}= \text{CH}_2 + \text{Base–H} + \text{X}^-
$$

Here, **R** is any carbon chain, **X** is the leaving group, and **Base⁻** is the strong base. The product is an alkene (the double bond) plus the conjugate acid of the base and the halide ion.

### Everyday comparison

Think of a two‑person tug‑of‑war where one side pulls a rope (the base pulling the hydrogen) while the other side simultaneously lets go of the rope’s anchor (the leaving group). The rope only snaps cleanly when both actions happen at the same moment and the participants stand opposite each other—just like the antiperiplanar requirement.

> **In daily life:** An E2 reaction is like opening a sliding door that has a latch on one side and a push bar on the other; you must push the bar (base) while releasing the latch (leaving group) at the same time for the door to glide open smoothly.

By keeping these ideas in mind—strong base, antiperiplanar geometry, and substrate structure—you can predict when an E2 elimination will be fast, slow, or unlikely, and you’ll be ready to apply this knowledge to real‑world organic synthesis.

sections.heading: 8. Factors Controlling Addition vs. Elimination
sections.body:
When a molecule that contains a carbon‑carbon double or triple bond meets a reagent, it can either **add** something across the bond (addition) or **remove** something and form a new double bond (elimination). Which path is taken does not happen by chance; it depends on several factors that we can think of as “rules of the road” for the reaction. Below we look at each rule, why it matters, and a simple everyday picture that helps you remember it.

> **Definition:** *Substrate* – the organic molecule that carries the double or triple bond and will undergo the reaction. We classify substrates by how many other carbon groups are attached to the carbon bearing the leaving group: primary (one), secondary (two), or tertiary (three).

A **primary** carbon is like a quiet side street: it has only one neighboring group, so it is less crowded. A **tertiary** carbon is like a busy intersection with three side roads; it is sterically (spatially) crowded but can stabilize positive charge very well. This difference matters because:

- In **E1** (unimolecular elimination) the first step creates a carbocation (a positively‑charged carbon). Tertiary carbocations are much more stable than secondary or primary ones, so E1 prefers tertiary substrates.
- In **E2** (bimolecular elimination) the base pulls a hydrogen away while the leaving group leaves at the same time. Here steric crowding can hinder the base from reaching the hydrogen, so primary substrates often give faster E2 reactions.

> **Note:** *Base* – a species that likes to accept a proton (H⁺). Strong bases (e.g., OH⁻, alkoxides) are eager proton grabbers; weak bases (e.g., water, alcohols) are less aggressive.

The **strength of the base** is a key switch:

- A **strong base** pushes the reaction toward elimination because it can efficiently pull a hydrogen away. Think of a strong base as a powerful vacuum cleaner that quickly removes the “hydrogen dust” from the substrate.
- A **weak base** is more likely to let the electrophile (electron‑loving species) add across the double bond, leading to addition. It’s like a gentle hand that lets a piece of clay (the electrophile) stick to the surface rather than pulling it away.

> **In daily life:** *Nucleophile vs. base* – A nucleophile is a “electron donor” that wants to attach to a positively charged site, while a base is a “proton snatcher.” Many molecules can be both, but their behavior changes with the reaction conditions. For example, the hydroxide ion (OH⁻) is both a strong base and a good nucleophile; in a polar protic solvent it often acts as a base, favoring elimination.

**Solvent polarity** also guides the outcome. Polar solvents (like water or methanol) stabilize ions, making it easier for charged intermediates such as carbocations to form. This stabilization helps E1 reactions because the first step is ion formation. Non‑polar solvents (like hexane) do not stabilize ions well, so addition reactions that proceed through neutral transition states become more competitive.

**Temperature** is another simple lever. Raising the temperature supplies extra kinetic energy, which favors elimination because elimination usually has a higher activation energy (the energy barrier that must be crossed). It’s similar to heating a pot of water: the hotter it gets, the more likely the water will boil off (eliminate) rather than stay as liquid (add).

**Leaving group ability** refers to how easily a group can depart with its electron pair. Good leaving groups (e.g., Br⁻, I⁻, tosylate) leave readily, making elimination easier. Poor leaving groups (e.g., –OH) require conversion (like turning –OH into –OTs) before elimination can happen. When the leaving group is excellent, the reaction can proceed by either addition or elimination, and the other factors (base strength, substrate, solvent) decide the path.

Putting the pieces together, we can write a simple decision “flow”:

$$
\text{If (strong base) \& (primary/secondary substrate) \& (high temperature)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{E2 elimination}
$$

$$
\text{If (weak base) \& (polar protic solvent) \& (stable carbocation possible)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{E1 elimination}
$$

$$
\text{If (weak nucleophile) \& (non‑polar solvent) \& (moderate temperature)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Electrophilic addition}
$$

> **Remember:** The outcome is rarely decided by a single factor; it is the combination of substrate structure, base strength, nucleophile vs. base character, solvent polarity, temperature, and leaving‑group quality that determines whether addition or elimination wins the race. By checking each “rule of the road,” you can predict and control the reaction you want.

sections.heading: 9. Practice Problems and Real‑World Examples
sections.body:
Predict the product of each reaction, decide whether the step proceeds by an **E1** (two‑step elimination) or **E2** (one‑step elimination) mechanism, and then see how the same chemistry is used in real‑world processes such as making plastics or medicines.

---

**Exercise 1 – Simple electrophilic addition**  

Write the major product when 1‑butene reacts with $HBr$ in the presence of peroxide (radical initiator).  

*Why it works:* The peroxide makes the addition follow a **radical** pathway, but the overall result is the same as a normal electrophilic addition – the $H$ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (the “less substituted” carbon) and $Br$ ends up on the more substituted carbon.  

> **Note:** In radical addition the order of $H$ and $Br$ is reversed compared with the classic “Markovnikov” rule for $HBr$ without peroxide.

---

**Exercise 2 – Electrophilic addition to an alkyne**  

Predict the product when acetylene ($HC\equiv CH$) is treated with excess $H_2$ in the presence of a palladium catalyst.  

*Why it works:* Hydrogenation adds $H_2$ across the triple bond in two steps. The first $H_2$ converts the alkyne to an alkene; the second $H_2$ turns the alkene into an alkane.  

> **Definition:** *Catalyst* – a substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed.

---

**Exercise 3 – Choose E1 or E2**  

A secondary alkyl bromide, $CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_3$, is heated with a weak base (pyridine). Which elimination mechanism occurs, and what is the major alkene product?  

*Reasoning:* A weak base cannot remove a proton in a single concerted step, so the reaction proceeds by the two‑step **E1** pathway: first the bromide leaves, forming a carbocation; then the base removes a proton from the adjacent carbon. The most stable alkene (more substituted) is formed.  

> **Remember:** E1 favors more stable carbocations and gives the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene.

---

**Exercise 4 – Choose E1 or E2 (harder)**  

The same substrate $CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_3$ is now treated with a strong, bulky base (tert‑butoxide, $t$‑BuO⁻) at low temperature. Which mechanism operates, and what alkene is produced?  

*Reasoning:* A strong, bulky base can abstract a proton while the leaving group departs in a single concerted step → **E2**. Because the base is bulky, it prefers to remove the less hindered (primary) hydrogen, giving the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product).  

> **Common mistake:** Assuming E2 always gives the more substituted alkene; steric bulk of the base can reverse the selectivity.

---

**Exercise 5 – Polymerization (real‑world example)**  

Ethylene ($CH_2=CH_2$) is polymerized using a metal‑oxide catalyst to form polyethylene. Write the repeating unit of the polymer and name the type of reaction involved.  

*Explanation:* Each ethylene molecule adds to the growing chain by an **addition** reaction (specifically, a chain‑growth polymerization). The double bond opens and links to the next monomer, repeating indefinitely.  

> **In daily life:** Polyethylene is the plastic used for grocery bags, milk jugs, and many other common items.

---

**Exercise 6 – Drug synthesis (real‑world example)**  

A pharmaceutical chemist needs to convert a secondary alcohol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3$, into the corresponding alkene for further functionalisation. They use concentrated $H_2SO_4$ and heat.  

1. Identify the mechanism (E1 or E2).  
2. Draw the major alkene product.  

*Reasoning:* Strong acid protonates the alcohol, turning it into a good leaving group (water). The reaction proceeds via an **E1** mechanism: loss of water forms a carbocation, then a base (often the conjugate base of the acid) removes a proton. The more substituted alkene is favored.  

> **Definition:** *Carbocation* – a positively charged carbon atom that is electron‑deficient and highly reactive.

---

**Putting it together – why these skills matter**  

Understanding when a reaction adds atoms (addition) versus removes them (elimination) lets chemists design molecules for specific purposes. In industry, addition reactions build long chains (plastics, synthetic rubber), while elimination reactions create double bonds that can be further functionalised (drug intermediates, fragrances). By practicing prediction and mechanism choice, you develop the intuition needed to read reaction maps and to troubleshoot real‑world syntheses.

examples.title: Hydrogenation of an Alkene
examples.given: 1‑hexene is treated with H₂/Pt. Identify the type of reaction and the product formed.

steps.label: Identify reactant
steps.text: Recognize 1‑hexene has a C=C double bond, which can undergo addition.

steps.label: Choose reagent action
steps.text: H₂ with a Pt catalyst adds across the double bond (electrophilic addition).

steps.label: Write product
steps.text: The double bond becomes a single bond, giving hexane (C₆H₁₄).

examples.answer: The reaction is an electrophilic addition (hydrogenation) producing hexane, C₆H₁₄.

examples.title: E2 Elimination of 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane with NaOEt
examples.given: 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane reacts with sodium ethoxide (NaOEt) in ethanol. Determine the reaction mechanism and the major alkene product.

steps.label: Examine substrate
steps.text: The carbon bearing Br is tertiary and has β‑hydrogens on adjacent carbons.

steps.label: Identify base strength
steps.text: NaOEt is a strong, non‑bulky base, favoring a concerted elimination (E2).

steps.label: Locate β‑hydrogen
steps.text: The most substituted β‑hydrogen leads to the more substituted double bond (Zaitsev’s rule).

steps.label: Draw product
steps.text: Removal of H from the β‑carbon and Br from the α‑carbon gives 2‑methyl‑2‑butene as the major alkene.

examples.answer: The reaction follows an E2 mechanism and the major product is 2‑methyl‑2‑butene (CH₃‑C(CH₃)=CH‑CH₃).

examples.title: Competing Addition vs. Elimination in 3‑bromo‑1‑pentene with H₂SO₄
examples.given: 3‑bromo‑1‑pentene is treated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 80 °C. Decide whether addition or elimination predominates and name the main product.

steps.label: Analyze substrate
steps.text: The molecule has both a C=C double bond (at C1‑C2) and a C–Br bond at C3.

steps.label: Consider reagent conditions
steps.text: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a strong acid that can protonate alkenes (addition) and also act as a dehydrating agent (promotes elimination).

steps.label: Evaluate temperature effect
steps.text: At 80 °C, elimination (E1) is favored over addition because higher temperature favors product stability (more substituted alkene).

steps.label: Predict mechanism
steps.text: Protonation of the alcohol‑like intermediate leads to loss of H₂O and formation of a carbocation at C3, followed by loss of Br⁻ to give a double bond.

steps.label: Identify product
steps.text: The most stable alkene formed is 1‑pentene (C=C between C1 and C2) after removal of HBr from C2‑C3.

examples.answer: Elimination (E1) predominates; the main product is 1‑pentene, CH₂=CH‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CH₃.

practice.q: Add HBr to 1‑butene. What is the major product?
practice.a: 1‑butene has the double bond between C‑1 and C‑2. In electrophilic addition of HBr, the H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (C‑1), forming a carbocation on C‑2. Br⁻ then attacks the carbocation. The product is 2‑bromobutane.

practice.q: What type of reaction converts 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol to 2‑methyl‑1‑butene when heated with sulfuric acid?
practice.a: Heating a secondary alcohol with a strong acid removes water. The –OH group is protonated, water leaves forming a carbocation on C‑2. A base (the conjugate base of H₂SO₄) removes a β‑hydrogen from C‑1, forming a double bond between C‑1 and C‑2. This is an E1 elimination, giving 2‑methyl‑1‑butene.

practice.q: Predict the product(s) and major regioselectivity when HCl adds to 2‑butyne. Show the mechanism.
practice.a: 2‑Butyne is a symmetrical internal alkyne (CH₃‑C≡C‑CH₃). In electrophilic addition of HCl, the π‑bond attacks H⁺, forming a vinyl cation. Because the alkyne is symmetrical, the cation can be placed on either carbon, but the more stable vinyl cation has the positive charge on the carbon bearing the methyl group (secondary). Chloride then attacks that carbon. The product is trans‑2‑chloro‑2‑butene (major) and a small amount of cis‑2‑chloro‑2‑butene. Mechanism steps: 1) π‑bond → H⁺ → vinyl cation; 2) Cl⁻ attack → C‑Cl bond formation.

practice.q: A substrate CH₃CH₂CH₂Br is treated with a strong base (NaOEt) in ethanol. Predict the major product and explain whether the reaction follows E1 or E2.
practice.a: The substrate is a primary alkyl bromide. Strong base and polar aprotic conditions favor a concerted bimolecular elimination (E2). The base abstracts a β‑hydrogen (from C‑2) while the C‑Br bond breaks simultaneously, forming a double bond between C‑1 and C‑2. The major product is 1‑propene. No carbocation intermediate forms, confirming an E2 mechanism.

practice.q: For the reaction of 3‑methyl‑1‑pentene with H₂SO₄ followed by H₂O, draw the product(s) and explain the Markovnikov vs. anti‑Markovnikov outcome. Include any possible rearrangements.
practice.a: 3‑Methyl‑1‑pentene has the double bond at the terminal position (CH₂=CH‑CH₂‑CH(CH₃)‑CH₃). H₂SO₄ adds H⁺ to the less substituted carbon (C‑1) giving a secondary carbocation at C‑2 (CH₃‑CH⁺‑CH₂‑CH(CH₃)‑CH₃). No hydride shift is needed because the carbocation is already secondary. Water then attacks the carbocation, and deprotonation yields 3‑methyl‑2‑pentanol as the major product (Markovnikov addition). Anti‑Markovnikov addition does not occur under these conditions because the acid catalyst directs the proton to the less substituted carbon.

practice.q: A secondary alkyl chloride, CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH₃, is heated with alcoholic KOH. Predict the product distribution (E2 vs. substitution) and draw the major elimination product, explaining stereochemical considerations.
practice.a: Alcoholic KOH is a strong, bulky base that favors elimination over substitution. The substrate is secondary, so E2 is preferred. The base removes a β‑hydrogen anti‑periplanar to the C‑Cl bond. Two sets of β‑hydrogens exist: on C‑1 (CH₃) and on C‑4 (CH₃). The anti‑periplanar geometry is best with the hydrogen on C‑4, leading to the more substituted double bond between C‑2 and C‑3. The major product is trans‑2‑pentene (the more stable E‑alkene). Minor product could be cis‑2‑pentene, but trans dominates due to lower steric strain. No substitution product is observed because the base is not nucleophilic enough for SN2 on a secondary carbon.

data.recap: The lesson covered unsaturated hydrocarbons, explaining how π bonds in alkenes and alkynes are weaker than σ bonds and can be broken in addition reactions. Electrophilic addition to alkenes proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, while alkynes can add twice to become fully saturated. Elimination reactions are the reverse process, with E1 occurring in two steps via a carbocation and E2 happening in one concerted step. Factors such as substrate structure and reaction conditions determine whether addition or elimination dominates.

key_terms.meaning: A bond formed by side‑by‑side overlap of p‑orbitals, weaker and located above and below the σ bond axis.
A strong head‑on overlap of orbitals that forms the primary bond between two atoms.
A reaction where an electron‑poor species adds to a multiple bond, creating a carbocation intermediate.
A positively charged carbon atom with only six valence electrons, formed when a leaving group departs.
A two‑step elimination where the leaving group leaves first, forming a carbocation, followed by deprotonation to give a double bond.
A one‑step, concerted elimination where a base removes a β‑hydrogen while the leaving group departs simultaneously.
In addition of HX to an alkene, the hydrogen adds to the less substituted carbon and the halide to the more substituted carbon.

key_terms.per: In radical‑initiated addition of HBr, the bromine adds to the less substituted carbon, opposite to the Markovnikov rule.

quiz.q: What type of bond is broken first in an addition reaction to an alkene?
quiz.why: The π bond is weaker and reacts first, allowing two new σ bonds to form.

quiz.q: In electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, which carbon initially receives the hydrogen?
quiz.why: Hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (less substituted) following Markovnikov's rule.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes an E1 reaction?
quiz.why: E1 proceeds via loss of the leaving group to give a carbocation, then deprotonation.

quiz.q: What is required for an E2 mechanism to occur efficiently?
options: A strong base and a good leaving group
quiz.why: E2 needs a strong base to abstract the β‑hydrogen while the leaving group departs.

quiz.q: When an alkyne undergoes addition of H₂ across the triple bond, what is the immediate product?
quiz.why: The first addition converts the alkyne to an alkene, leaving one π bond remaining.

quiz.q: In radical‑initiated addition of HBr to 1‑butene, where does bromine end up?
quiz.why: Radical addition follows anti‑Markovnikov orientation, placing Br on the less substituted (terminal) carbon.

flashcards.back: A bond formed by side‑by‑side overlap of parallel p‑orbitals, weaker than a σ bond and located above/below the bond axis.

flashcards.front: What happens to the π bond in an addition reaction?
flashcards.back: It breaks, allowing two new σ bonds to form with the incoming atoms or groups.
A positively charged carbon atom with only six valence electrons, usually formed after a leaving group departs.

flashcards.front: Key difference between E1 and E2 mechanisms?
flashcards.back: E1 is two‑step with a carbocation intermediate; E2 is one‑step, concerted, with base and leaving group acting simultaneously.

flashcards.front: State the Markovnikov rule for HX addition to alkenes.
flashcards.back: Hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (less substituted), and the halide adds to the more substituted carbon.
A radical‑initiated addition where the halogen adds to the less substituted carbon, opposite to the Markovnikov rule.

flashcards.front: Why can alkynes undergo two successive addition reactions?
flashcards.back: Because they have two π bonds; the first addition converts the alkyne to an alkene, leaving a second π bond for a second addition.

flashcards.front: Give an example of a good leaving group in elimination reactions.
flashcards.back: Halides such as bromide (Br⁻) or tosylate (OTs) are common good leaving groups.
